name: Evans syndrome
aliases: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia with immune thrombocytopenia

clinicalPearls: Defined by the combination of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia, either simultaneously or sequentially
Some patients also develop autoimmune neutropenia, reflecting broad autoantibody-mediated destruction of blood cells
The direct antiglobulin test is positive, and patients show both haemolysis and thrombocytopenic bleeding tendency
Frequently secondary to an underlying disorder such as lupus, lymphoproliferative disease or a primary immunodeficiency
It follows a relapsing and remitting course and is often more refractory to treatment than isolated autoimmune cytopenias
First-line treatment is corticosteroids, with immunoglobulin, rituximab and other immunosuppression used for relapse
Children presenting with Evans syndrome warrant evaluation for an underlying immune dysregulation disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Evans syndrome represents a breakdown of immune tolerance that generates autoantibodies against more than one blood-cell lineage. Warm IgG autoantibodies coat red cells, which are cleared extravascularly by splenic macrophages to cause haemolytic anaemia, while separate antiplatelet autoantibodies drive splenic destruction of platelets producing immune thrombocytopenia; some patients also form antineutrophil antibodies. The underlying immune dysregulation may be idiopathic or secondary to systemic autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders or inherited defects of immune regulation such as autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome and common variable immunodeficiency. The multilineage nature of the autoimmunity accounts for the relapsing course and the frequent need for prolonged immunosuppression.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or immune thrombocytopenia
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film demonstrating anaemia with spherocytes and thrombocytopenia
Haemolysis markers including reticulocytes, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and bilirubin
Autoimmune screen and investigation for systemic lupus erythematosus
Evaluation for lymphoproliferative disease and, in children, for primary immunodeficiency
Coagulation screen and assessment to exclude thrombotic microangiopathy
redFlags: Severe thrombocytopenia with significant or intracranial bleeding
Rapidly falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic compromise
Features suggesting thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura that require urgent exclusion
Evidence of an aggressive underlying lymphoproliferative disorder
reference.prognosis: The syndrome typically runs a chronic, relapsing course that is often harder to control than isolated autoimmune cytopenias, with outcome shaped by the response to immunosuppression and by any underlying disease.
pitfalls: Treating the anaemia or thrombocytopenia in isolation without recognising the combined syndrome
Missing an underlying autoimmune, lymphoproliferative or immunodeficiency disorder
Failing to consider thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura before attributing cytopenias to autoimmunity
Underestimating the relapsing course and stopping immunosuppression prematurely
management: First-line corticosteroids to suppress autoantibody-mediated destruction of red cells and platelets
Intravenous immunoglobulin for rapid control of severe immune thrombocytopenia or bleeding
Rituximab for relapsing or corticosteroid-refractory disease

Second-line immunosuppression (ciclosporin, mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine) and thrombopoietin-receptor agonists for a refractory thrombocytopenic component, with splenectomy considered in selected cases
Supportive care: folate supplementation, judicious transfusion of best-matched blood given the positive direct antiglobulin test, and careful haemostatic support
Investigate for and treat an underlying disorder such as systemic lupus erythematosus, lymphoproliferative disease or primary immunodeficiency (ALPS, CVID)
Monitor full blood count and haemolysis markers for relapse under long-term haematology follow-up
